title: I had losses and want to offset them
excerpt: How crypto asset losses are offset against gains, including gains on shares and funds, how long you have to do it and why a loss you don't declare is a loss you lose.

hero.etiqueta: What you've already lost can still count
hero.h1: You sold at a loss and now you have gains
hero.subheading: It might be a disastrous sale three years ago that you'd rather forget, and a good result in crypto or on the stock market this year. Those two things can be set against each other, but only if the loss was declared at the time.

sections.entrada: The rules that govern offsetting. The exact amounts and applicable limits depend on the tax year and need to be checked.

sections.body:
The loss usually has a similar story. You bought high, held on, ended up selling badly, and since the result was negative you assumed there was nothing to declare. It's the most natural reasoning in the world, and it's exactly the one that proves costly.

A declared capital loss is a tax asset: it is offset against gains in the same tax year and, if any is left over, against gains in the following years within the legal time limit. A loss that was not declared simply doesn't exist for these purposes.

And there's a detail many people don't know: offsetting doesn't distinguish between types of asset in the way you might expect. A loss from selling crypto can be set against a gain from selling shares or units in a fund, because what matters is not what you sold but which block of the tax base the result goes into.

steps.title: We review your previous tax returns
steps.body: We look for loss balances still waiting to be offset that you may not even know you had. They turn up more often than you'd think.

steps.title: We reconstruct the transactions behind the loss
steps.body: So that it can be proven: date, acquisition and disposal value, and the supporting documents. A loss without support is hard to sustain if it is reviewed.

steps.title: We check the time limit
steps.body: How much life each outstanding balance has left. Losses expire, and using them in the right order can prevent one from being lost along the way.

steps.title: We integrate crypto with the rest of your portfolio
steps.body: Shares, funds, derivatives. The offsetting rules link them, and applying them separately leaves money on the table.

steps.title: And if the loss was never declared, we assess the options
steps.body: There may be scope to amend tax years that are not yet time-barred. We tell you whether it's worth trying in your case.

items.q: I lost on crypto and gained on the stock market. Can they be set against each other?
items.a: Yes, provided both results go into the same block of the tax base, which is usually the case for gains and losses from disposals. What matters is not the type of asset but where the result is included.

items.q: I didn't declare the loss at the time
items.a: If the tax year is not time-barred, there may be scope to request an amendment and bring the loss to light. It isn't always worth the effort, and it depends on the amount and the tax years involved. We analyse it before doing anything.

items.q: I sold at a loss and bought back shortly afterwards
items.a: There are specific rules that restrict counting the loss when homogeneous assets — essentially the same asset — are bought back within certain periods. It's a point worth reviewing with the exact dates in front of you, because it changes the result.

items.q: What if I lost money because an exchange went bust?
items.a: That's a different situation from a sale at a loss, and its treatment isn't automatic: it depends on how and when the loss of the right can be evidenced. It deserves its own analysis and specific documentation.

items.q: How much time do I have?
items.a: The general period for offsetting against gains in later tax years is four years. That's why it's worth reviewing outstanding balances every year and not letting them expire unused.
